description:
PyTop | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we aim to collaborate on an intuitive and informative solution that helps users compare lunar landing sites and dates through clear visualizations of relevant lunar environmental conditions.

Our interests: Python, AI/ML, web development, data visualization, astronomy, and scientific problem-solving.

Looking for teammates: We welcome collaborators with interests or experience in astronomy, physics, mathematics, scientific data analysis, UI/UX design, and interactive visualization.

Our goal is to combine technical skills, scientific reasoning, and teamwork to develop a useful, accessible solution.
summary:
PyTop built LunaSpan for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It lets users compare lunar landing sites and dates by showing when the Sun and Earth are both above the modeled horizon. For a solar-powered lander, that overlap is a useful first check for when sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth might coincide.

In our six-hour south-pole example, Shackleton Rim has 3 hours 34 minutes of overlap, while de Gerlache Rim 1 has 6 hours—a difference of 2 hours 26 minutes. Side-by-side timelines, elevation charts, and interactive 3D views help users see what drives that difference. LunaSpan is designed for early planning and teaching, not to guarantee power or radio contact. It also includes a separate planner for Moon viewing and dark-sky windows from Earth.
details:
LunaSpan addresses a practical question in the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: what changes if a mission moves to another landing site or its arrival slips? Users can choose a preset or enter their own lunar coordinates, set a UTC time range, and compare two sites or two dates at one site. The planner shows Sun and Earth elevations, sunlight and darkness intervals, Earth visibility, and the time when both bodies are above the modeled horizon. Users can inspect the timelines, export CSV files, and share a comparison link.

In our south-pole comparison, both sites use the same interval: 14 December 2026 at 20:00 UTC to 15 December at 02:00 UTC. Shackleton Rim has 3 h 34 min of overlap because Earth starts below the modeled horizon. At de Gerlache Rim 1, both bodies stay above it for the full 6 h. The Athena example demonstrates a schedule change: moving the same four-day window three days later increases the modeled overlap from 92.1 h to 96.0 h.

We built the web app with Python, FastAPI, Skyfield, NumPy, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js. The calculation engine uses NASA JPL’s DE440s ephemeris and lunar orientation kernels. We cross-checked selected calculations against JPL Horizons. The 3D views use NASA Moon imagery and measured LRO/LOLA elevation data for the two featured south-pole sites. Linked clocks let users explore both scenarios at the same relative point in their timelines. The separate Earth observation planner finds Moon-viewing and dark-sky windows in the selected location’s local time.

LunaSpan is intended for early scenario comparison and education. Measured terrain is used for visualization, not to calculate shadows or terrain-obstructed visibility. The planner does not predict solar power output, radio-link reliability, or weather.

SI disclosure: PyTop used Claude and ChatGPT to assist with drafting, debugging, and integrating parts of the calculation code and interactive 3D interface. ChatGPT also assisted with documentation and submission wording. The team integrated and tested the application. The credited NASA imagery, elevation data, and JPL kernels are sourced datasets, not SI-generated data.
